title: Tech Debt Crisis
narrative:
You're senior now. And the tech debt is real.

The codebase has accumulated 3 years of "quick fixes." Half the tests are flaky. The deployment pipeline takes 45 minutes. New hires quit after a week.

Your manager says: "We need to ship features, not fix old code." But you know: without paying down tech debt, shipping features will get slower and slower.

You need to make the case.

choices.text: Propose a dedicated tech debt sprint

success.text: You present data: tech debt is causing 40% of all bugs. Management agrees to a 2-week cleanup sprint. The team morale improves dramatically.
success.log: Convinced leadership to fund tech debt cleanup!

failure.text: Management says "we'll get to it next quarter." They always say that. You sigh and go back to feature work.

choices.text: Fix it quietly while shipping features

success.text: You refactor small pieces as you go. It's exhausting but the codebase slowly improves. Your team notices.

failure.text: You try to fix things but feature work always takes priority. You're burned out and the codebase is worse than ever.
failure.log: Burned out trying to fix everything.

choices.text: Profile the system, find the real bottleneck

success.text: You profile the deploy pipeline and find 31 of the 45 minutes is one untested step that could be cached. You fix that first, with zero feature impact. Now when you make the case for a debt sprint, you lead with "I already cut deploy time by 70%."
success.log: Cut deploy time 70%. Now the case writes itself.

failure.text: You profile for a week and find the real bottleneck: the database, which is owned by another team with a six-week queue. Your findings are correct, actionable, and entirely outside your control.
failure.log: Found the bottleneck. It's someone else's database.

title: The Interview Panel
narrative:
You're on the engineering interview panel. A candidate is about to come in for a technical interview.

You've been given a coding problem to administer. The problem is... you know it's a terrible problem. It tests trivia, not engineering ability.

The company standard says "use this exact problem." But you know good engineers when you see them.

choices.text: Use the standard problem but adapt it

success.text: You follow the letter of the policy but add real-world context. The candidate shines. You hire them. They become a great teammate.

failure.text: The candidate is good but the problem doesn't showcase their strengths. They perform poorly. You reject them. Two months later, a competitor hires them as a senior.
failure.log: Rejected a good candidate. Bad hire decision.

choices.text: Reject the standard problem and design your own

success.text: You design a realistic system design exercise. The candidate loves it. They show their true abilities. You hire them.
success.log: Better interview process led to great hire!

failure.text: Your manager says you broke protocol. The candidate is confused by your unstructured format. Nobody's happy.

choices.text: Solve the problem yourself, on the spot

success.text: Before the candidate arrives, you solve the standard problem — and it takes 40 minutes of genuine work, not the 15 the rubric assumes. You show the panel where the problem breaks. The panel lead quietly swaps in a better question. The candidate gets a fair interview. Engineering gets a better hire.
success.log: Solved the problem, exposed the rubric.

failure.text: You solve it in 40 minutes and present your findings, but the panel lead insists the problem is "fine as designed." You interview with a bad question and a bad feeling, and the candidate tells everyone about it.
failure.log: Proved the problem was broken. Nobody cared.

title: Burnout Warning Signs
narrative:
You've been working 60+ hour weeks for 3 months. Your code quality is slipping. You're irritable in meetings. You check Slack in your dreams.

Your doctor says: "You need to reduce stress." Your partner says: "You need to be present." Your team lead says: "We're worried about you."

But there's a major release next week.

choices.text: Take a week off. Unplug completely.

success.text: You hand off your responsibilities. The team manages fine. You come back refreshed and your code quality doubles. Your team respects you for prioritizing health.
success.log: Took time off. Came back stronger!

failure.text: You try to disconnect but the release needs you. You spend the week "off" answering Slack messages. It's the worst of both worlds.

choices.text: Delegate more and set boundaries

success.text: You delegate effectively and say "no" to non-essential work. Your team steps up. You maintain work-life balance and the release ships.

failure.text: You try to delegate but nobody else knows the system. You end up doing more work teaching others. The release is stressful.

choices.text: Push through. It's just one more release.

success.text: Against all odds, you power through. The release ships. But you're running on fumes. The victory feels hollow.
success.log: Survived the release but at a cost.

failure.text: You collapse. Not dramatically — just a bad week of illness. The release is delayed. Your team covers for you but trust is damaged.

title: Performance Review
narrative:
It's performance review season. Your manager calls you into a meeting (or Zoom call). They have a document.

"Let's talk about your year. You've delivered well on most projects. Your code quality has improved. However..."

The "however" is coming.

choices.text: Prepare your accomplishments in advance

success.text: You present a well-documented list of achievements. Your manager is impressed. You get a strong rating and a raise.

failure.text: You wing it. Your manager has a different view of your year. The rating is lower than expected.

choices.text: Ask for honest feedback

success.text: You get candid, useful feedback. You create a growth plan. Your manager respects your maturity.

failure.text: The feedback is harsh and unconstructive. "You need more visibility." Translation: "You need to be more political."

choices.text: Bring the bugs you caught before shipping

success.text: You bring a one-pager: 14 production incidents avoided this year, each with the PR where you caught it. The "however" in the manager's document loses its momentum. "These are great," they say, "let's make sure they're visible to the whole org." You've turned a review into a promotion artifact.

failure.text: You bring the list, but three of the 14 were caught by CI, not you, and the manager knows it. The review proceeds, and you've learned to double-check your authorship claims.
failure.log: Three of the 14 were CI's, not yours.

title: Conference Talk Opportunity
narrative:
Your company is sending 3 people to a major tech conference. Your manager asks who wants to go and present.

Public speaking terrifies you. But it's a career opportunity. The conference has 5,000 attendees and industry leaders.

Your coworker who loves attention is also interested.

choices.text: Say yes and prepare rigorously

success.text: You practice for weeks. Your talk is excellent. You meet industry leaders. Your career gets a huge boost.

failure.text: You freeze on stage. It's awkward. But... people were kind. You learn and come back stronger next year.
failure.log: Conference talk was rough but you learned.

choices.text: Nominate your extroverted coworker

success.text: Your coworker absolutely crushes it. They thank you for the opportunity. You look like a team player.

failure.text: Your coworker steals your thunder. They mention your work in their talk and get all the credit. You're not mad. (You're a little mad.)

choices.text: Do a live coding demo instead of slides

success.text: You skip the slides and build the feature live on stage, in front of 5,000 people. It compiles on the first try. The room goes quiet in the best way. A maintainer from a major framework DMs you after: "How did you do that?"
success.log: Live demo. Compiled first try. Legend status.

failure.text: You go live coding. Of course it doesn't compile. You debug on stage for six minutes while 5,000 people watch, and the talk becomes a story everyone tells — but not the way you'd tell it.
failure.log: Live demo. Six minutes of on-stage debugging.

title: The Promotion Review
narrative:
It's promotion review season. You're up for Senior → Staff.

Your manager says: "You need more visibility. You need to influence at a higher level. You need to..."

You look at your coworker who just gave a talk at a major conference. They're already getting their promotion packet.

You've spent 6 months deep in the code. Nobody knows what you've built.

choices.text: Write a detailed impact report

success.text: You write a compelling report showing your impact. Your manager is impressed. You get the promotion.

failure.text: Your report is too technical. Your manager doesn't understand it. You wait another quarter.

choices.text: Start giving talks and writing blog posts

success.text: You give a talk at an internal tech day. People are impressed. You get invited to speak externally.

failure.text: Nobody shows up to your talk. 3 people attend. One is your manager.

choices.text: Document the incidents you led

success.text: You write the postmortems nobody else wanted to write: what broke, why, what you changed. Six months of invisible work becomes a portfolio. Your manager forwards the stack to the Staff committee with one line: "This is why." The visibility problem solves itself.
success.log: Six months of invisible work, documented.

failure.text: You write the docs, but they're accurate to a fault — including the incident where your fix made things worse for a week. The Staff committee reads all of it. The promotion is "next cycle."

title: The Security Audit
narrative:
The security team just finished their audit. Your service has 237 vulnerabilities. 12 are critical.

The worst one: your API keys are hardcoded in the source code. They've been public on GitHub for 6 months.

The CISO wants a meeting. Tomorrow.

choices.text: Own it and fix everything

success.text: You admit the mistakes and present a remediation plan. The CISO respects your honesty. You fix everything in 2 weeks.

failure.text: The CISO is furious. They want your head. You're assigned to security work for the next 6 months.

choices.text: Blame the legacy code

success.text: You blame the legacy codebase. The CISO buys it. You get a pass. (You're a little ashamed.)

failure.text: The CISO knows you wrote the code. They don't buy the excuse. You're in trouble.

choices.text: Find and fix the vulnerabilities yourself

success.text: You triage all 237 before the CISO's meeting: 12 critical, 141 that are misconfigured scanners, 84 that are "theoretical." You rotate the API keys in an hour and walk the CISO through the real list. "237" becomes "12," and the meeting goes from tribunal to work session.

failure.text: You triage the list and find the scanner missed the real problem: a second set of keys, in a config file, public for two years. You fix it, but the CISO's meeting is now about why the audit missed it, and the audit was your team's process.
failure.log: Found the keys the scanner missed. Two years old.

title: The Keynote Invitation
narrative:
You've been invited to give a keynote at a major tech conference. 3,000 attendees. Industry leaders in the audience.

Your topic: "How we scaled our platform to 10 million users."

You've never given a keynote. You've barely given a talk.

Your hands are shaking.

choices.text: Practice like your life depends on it

success.text: You practice for weeks. The keynote is a hit. People approach you after with job offers.

failure.text: You freeze on stage. It's painful. But people were kind. You learn and come back stronger.
failure.log: Freeze on stage. But you learned.

choices.text: Hire a professional speaker coach

success.text: The coach helps you find your voice. The keynote is great. You're a natural.
success.log: Speaker coach made you a pro!

failure.text: The coach is a scam. You waste $5,000 and still freeze on stage.

choices.text: Write the demo code so it actually works

success.text: You build the scaling demo end-to-end, run it 40 times, and record it as a fallback. On stage, the live version works. When you say "10 million users," the graph behind you is real. The Q&A is the best of your career, because every answer is grounded in code you've actually written.
success.log: The demo was real. The Q&A carried you.

failure.text: You build the demo, but it needs a 47-step setup that only works on your machine. On stage, step 31 fails. You fall back to the recording, which is fine, until the venue's playback system decides it wants to be a video conference.
failure.log: The demo needed 47 steps. Step 31 had other plans.

title: The KPI Trap
narrative:
Your manager introduces new KPIs: lines of code committed, PRs merged per week, tickets closed.

You've been writing careful, well-tested code. This will make you look bad.

Your coworker who writes spaghetti code is now the top performer.

The CEO loves the dashboard.

choices.text: Push back on the KPIs

success.text: You present data showing KPIs don't correlate with quality. Your manager listens. KPIs are changed.

failure.text: Your manager says "the CEO loves the dashboard." You're told to adapt.

choices.text: Game the KPIs

success.text: You break features into tiny PRs. Your KPIs look great. You feel dirty but you're #1.

failure.text: Your manager notices the tiny PRs. They ask why you're not shipping features.

choices.text: Instrument the system, measure the real numbers

success.text: You build a dashboard that measures what actually matters: change lead time, failure rate, recovery time. You don't argue with the KPIs — you just make them visible. Two sprints later, the CEO asks why the spaghetti coder's "output" correlates with the incident channel. The KPIs quietly evolve.
success.log: Instrumented the real metrics. The KPIs evolved.

failure.text: You build the dashboard, but the CEO's favorite metric — PRs per week — lives on a different dashboard, in a different tool, that you don't have admin access to. Your truth is now a side project.
failure.log: Your dashboard lost to the CEO's dashboard.

title: The On-Call Nightmare
narrative:
It's your on-call week. Your phone buzzes at 3 AM.

"Database is down. Users can't log in. The CEO is calling."

You've been on-call for 3 weeks straight. You're exhausted.

The database cluster has 47 nodes. You don't know which one is failing.

choices.text: Diagnose systematically

success.text: You methodically check each node. You find the failing one. You restart it. Database recovers.

failure.text: You check nodes randomly. You waste 2 hours. The CEO calls again.

choices.text: Call the DBA team

success.text: The DBA team fixes it in 15 minutes. You learn the root cause. You're on-call again next week.

failure.text: The DBA team is asleep. You wait 45 minutes. The CEO is furious.

choices.text: Find the bug and fix it yourself

success.text: You stop diagnosing and start reading: the failing node is running a config from last year's deploy. You roll it back, the cluster heals in 20 minutes, and the CEO's call goes to voicemail. You write the postmortem before your coffee gets cold.

failure.text: You find the failing node and fix it, but the cluster fails over to a second node with the same stale config. You're now in hour three, and the CEO has stopped calling because the support queue has started numbering the requests.
failure.log: Fixed one node. The cluster had two.

title: The Blameless Retrospective
narrative:
A production incident just happened. Your team is in a retrospective.

The manager says: "This is a blameless retrospective. Let's focus on process, not people."

But everyone is looking at you. You deployed the bad code. You missed the test. You should have caught it.

The silence is deafening.

choices.text: Own your mistake publicly

success.text: You admit your mistake and propose process improvements. Your team respects your honesty.
success.log: Owned the mistake. Team respected you!

failure.text: You admit your mistake but your manager takes it too far. They make it about you, not process.

choices.text: Stay quiet and let it pass

success.text: Nobody mentions you. The retrospective moves on. You learn privately.

failure.text: Your coworker mentions you. "John deployed the bad code." The room turns to you.

choices.text: Present the postmortem with the data

success.text: You open the postmortem: the deploy timeline, the test that should have caught it, the monitoring gap. No names, all facts. The room shifts from "whose fault" to "which of these do we fix first." You leave with three action items assigned before the coffee's done.

failure.text: You present the data, but the monitoring gap turns out to be a budget item, not a process item. The retro ends with "we'll look into it," and you've spent your credibility on a fix that needs a purchase order.
failure.log: The fix needs a budget, not a process.

title: The Architecture Presentation
narrative:
You've designed a new architecture. It's elegant, scalable, and perfect.

You're presenting it to the engineering team. They have questions.

"What about latency?" "What about cost?" "What about our existing infrastructure?"

You didn't think about those.

choices.text: Admit you didn't consider those factors

success.text: You admit the gaps. The team helps you fill them. The architecture gets better.

failure.text: You deflect. The team doesn't buy it. Your credibility takes a hit.

choices.text: Push back on the concerns

success.text: You address each concern with data. The team is convinced. The architecture ships.

failure.text: Your data is weak. The team pushes back harder. The architecture is delayed.

choices.text: Show the actual benchmarks

success.text: You pause the Q&A: "Give me an hour. I'll benchmark it." You do. At 4 PM you're back with numbers: latency, cost, and migration effort for each concern. The team's objections don't disappear, but they become decisions instead of vibes. The architecture ships with a risk table attached.

failure.text: You spend the hour benchmarking, but the test environment doesn't match production, and your numbers are off by 2x. The team trusts the process, not the numbers, and the architecture review is scheduled again. Next time you bring a recording.
failure.log: The benchmarks were 2x off. Review rescheduled.

title: The SVPG Product Model
narrative:
Your company is adopting the Silicon Valley Product Group (SVPG) model. The VP of Product just sent a 47-page deck.

It talks about "product-market fit," "the product lifecycle," and "the three horizons."

You don't know what any of this means. Your team lead says it means "product wants more features."

The new process: every feature needs a "Product Requirements Document" AND a "Success Metrics Framework" AND a "Go-to-Market Alignment."

Your simple bug fix now needs a 10-page doc.

choices.text: Learn the framework

success.text: You read the deck. You understand the SVPG model. You write a PRD that actually helps. Product respects you.

failure.text: You read the deck. You don't understand it. You write a 10-page PRD that nobody reads.

choices.text: Do the minimum required

success.text: You write a 2-page PRD. Product complains but approves it. You ship faster than everyone else.

failure.text: Product rejects your 2-page PRD. They want 10 pages. You're stuck in review for 2 weeks.

choices.text: Pilot the model on your own team first

success.text: You take one small feature and run the full SVPG gauntlet on it: PRD, metrics framework, GTM alignment. It takes three weeks for a two-week feature — and the doc is so good that product stops arguing with engineering about scope for a month. You've made the bureaucracy legible, and legible things get fixed.
success.log: Ran the gauntlet. Made the bureaucracy legible.

failure.text: You run the pilot, but the "Success Metrics Framework" requires 90 days of data to be meaningful. Your pilot is now a quarter-long project with a 10-page doc and no feature to show for it.
failure.log: The framework needs 90 days. The feature needed 2 weeks.

title: The Product Triangle
narrative:
Your VP of Product introduces the "Product Triangle": Fast, Good, Cheap. Pick two.

They say: "We want Fast AND Good. We're sorry, it's going to be expensive."

Your budget is cut 30%.

Your team lead says: "Just make it work."

The product team says: "We need it in 2 weeks."

The CEO says: "Make it great."

The Product Triangle is... a lie.

choices.text: Show them the triangle

success.text: You draw the triangle on a whiteboard. Everyone understands. They pick "Good and Cheap" and give you more time.

failure.text: The VP says "we're special. We can break the triangle." Nobody believes them.

choices.text: Just build what they ask

success.text: You build it. It's fast, it's good, and it's expensive. Your team burns out but ships.

failure.text: You can't make it work. The feature ships late, it's buggy, and it costs more than expected.

choices.text: Show the failure modes with real examples

success.text: You pull three past projects where "fast and good" was chosen: the launch that slipped 6 weeks, the one that shipped with a data migration bug, the one that quietly died. You put the actual numbers on the wall. The VP of Product is quiet for a long time. "Okay," they say. "What do you need?" The budget comes back at 20%.
success.log: Three failure modes, real numbers. Budget back at 20%.

failure.text: You present the failure modes, but the CEO heard one in the hallway and asks for "a version of that energy in the roadmap." The triangle survives. The budget doesn't. The team learns that data is a suggestion.

title: The Code of Conduct Incident
narrative:
A team member makes an inappropriate comment in a public channel. It's not terrible, but it's not okay.

The team is divided. Some think it's no big deal. Others are offended.

Your manager says: "Handle this. You're a senior engineer."

It's your call.

choices.text: Address it directly and privately

success.text: You talk to them privately. They apologize. The team moves on. Everyone respects your handling.
success.log: Handled it privately. Team respected you!

failure.text: You address it publicly. They get defensive. The situation gets worse.

choices.text: Let HR handle it

success.text: HR handles it professionally. You're not involved. The team moves on.

failure.text: HR takes 2 weeks. The team is simmering. Your manager asks why you didn't step in.

choices.text: Propose a team-wide CoC workshop to prevent future issues

success.text: The workshop is well-received. The team learns from the incident and improves their behavior. You're seen as a leader.

failure.text: The workshop falls flat. People are defensive. Nothing changes.

title: The Lucky Break
narrative:
A competitor just open-sourced their entire platform. It's exactly what you've been building — but they've done 6 months of work in 2 weeks.

Your team is excited. Your manager is nervous. The CEO wants to know if you can 'just copy it and ship faster.'

You know open-sourced code is a minefield — licenses, security, technical debt. But your team sees an opportunity.

choices.text: Audit the codebase thoroughly before considering anything

success.text: You find the code is poorly written and has licensing issues. You present this to the team and your manager. They respect your caution.

failure.text: You audit but miss a critical license violation. The company uses the code and gets sued.

choices.text: Use it as inspiration — build your own version faster

success.text: You use the open-source code as a reference and build a better version in half the time. Your team is motivated and the product is superior.

failure.text: You try to build faster but cut corners. The product has bugs and your team is frustrated.

choices.text: Ignore it — focus on your own roadmap

success.text: You ignore it. The competitor's code has a critical bug that gets exploited. Your decision to focus on your own roadmap was wise.

failure.text: You ignore it. The competitor's product goes viral. Your roadmap is irrelevant.

choices.text: Contribute back to the project — build a relationship

success.text: You contribute bug fixes and feature requests. The maintainers appreciate it. You get early access to improvements.

failure.text: Your contributions are rejected. The maintainers are hostile. You wasted time.

title: The Technical Deep Dive
narrative:
Your team is stuck on a performance issue that no one can solve. The database is slow, the API is slow, the frontend is slow.

You've been asked to take ownership. You have 2 weeks to find the root cause and fix it.

The issue is complex. It involves multiple systems, third-party integrations, and legacy code you didn't write.

choices.text: Spend 2 weeks deep in the code — find the root cause

success.text: You find the issue — a N+1 query in a library you didn't know existed. You fix it and add monitoring. Performance improves 10x.

failure.text: You spend 2 weeks but can't find the root cause. The issue persists. Your team is frustrated.

choices.text: Bring in an external consultant to help diagnose

success.text: The consultant finds the issue in 2 days. You learn from them and implement the fix. The team is impressed.

failure.text: The consultant is expensive and doesn't find much. You're out $10k and still stuck.

choices.text: Rewrite the affected system from scratch

success.text: You rewrite the system. It's faster, cleaner, and easier to maintain. The team loves it.

failure.text: The rewrite introduces new bugs. The system is slower than before. You revert.

choices.text: Accept the performance issue — it's not critical enough to fix

success.text: You accept it. The performance is bad but users adapt. You focus on other priorities.

failure.text: Users complain. The performance issue becomes a customer churn problem.

title: The Pivot
narrative:
Your product has been in development for 6 months. Today, the CEO announces a complete pivot — the product is going in a different direction.

All your work is going to be thrown away. The team is demoralized. Some engineers are already updating their resumes.

You have 2 weeks to redirect the team's effort. The old features are useless. The new direction is vague.

choices.text: Rally the team — focus on what we can reuse

success.text: You identify 60% of the codebase that's still useful. The team rebuilds faster than expected. The pivot succeeds.

failure.text: You try to reuse code but it doesn't fit the new direction. The team is stuck.

choices.text: Start fresh — build the new product from scratch

success.text: You build the new product from scratch. It's clean and fast. The team is proud of the work.

failure.text: The new product has bugs. The team is frustrated. The CEO is unhappy.

choices.text: Negotiate a hybrid — keep some old features, add new ones

success.text: You negotiate a hybrid approach. The old features that work stay. The new direction is added. Everyone is somewhat happy.

failure.text: The CEO says no. The pivot is complete. You're back to square one.

choices.text: Leave the company — this is too risky

success.text: You leave. The pivot fails. The company folds. You look like a genius.

failure.text: You leave. The pivot succeeds. The company goes public. You missed out.

title: The Random Bug
narrative:
A bug appears in production. It only happens on Tuesdays. It only affects 1% of users. It can't be reproduced in staging.

You've been assigned to fix it. The team is frustrated. The CEO is asking for updates.

You've tried everything — logs, metrics, user reports. Nothing explains the bug.

choices.text: Do a systematic investigation — check every variable

success.text: You find the bug — it's a race condition that only triggers on Tuesdays when a specific cron job runs. You fix it.

failure.text: You investigate but can't find the bug. The team is frustrated.

choices.text: Add more logging and wait for the next occurrence

success.text: You add logging. The bug happens again. The logs reveal the pattern. You fix it.

failure.text: The bug doesn't happen again. You're stuck.

choices.text: Guess at the fix — try something and see if it works

success.text: You guess that it's a memory leak. You add a restart schedule. The bug disappears. You don't know why it worked but it did.

failure.text: Your guess was wrong. The bug is still there. You've wasted time.

choices.text: Ask the team for help — collective brainpower

success.text: The team helps. They find the bug in 2 hours — it's a timezone issue that only affects Tuesdays. You fix it.

failure.text: The team can't find the bug. You're stuck.

title: BOSS: The Platform Rewrite
narrative:
Your BOSS. The CTO has declared the entire platform "architecturally unsound" and wants a complete rewrite in a new stack.

"The old system was built by amateurs," they say. (It was built by you and your team over 3 years.)

You're tasked with building the new platform. The old system has 2 million users. Downtime is NOT an option.

The rewrite challenge awaits.

choices.text: Build it right — proper architecture, proper testing

success.text: You design a beautiful, scalable architecture. The new platform is 10x faster, 10x more reliable. It takes 6 months but it's worth it. You've proven the old system's worth by building something even better.
success.log: Built a platform that outshines the old one!

failure.text: Perfection takes too long. The old system is still breaking while you're building the perfect new one. Leadership gets impatient.

choices.text: Ship a minimal viable platform and iterate

success.text: You ship the basics in 2 months. It's not perfect but it works. You iterate based on real usage. Leadership is impressed by the speed.

failure.text: The MVP is too minimal. It can't handle production load. You have to rebuild significant portions. Now you have TWO platforms.

choices.text: Push back — the old system works fine

success.text: You present data showing the old system is stable. You propose incremental improvements instead of a rewrite. The CTO backs down. Crisis averted.

failure.text: The CTO is unmoved. "I've made my decision." You're stuck leading a rewrite you think is unnecessary. Morale plummets.
